objectives: Predict-then-match Words-in-Context to beat the familiar-meaning trap
Answer purpose/structure questions with a functional verb
Pin each author's stance before Cross-Text comparison

slides.title: Part 1 — From 'what' to 'how & why'
slides.body: Craft & Structure (~28% of Reading & Writing) stops asking what a passage says and starts asking how it is built and why the author made each move. Different question, different reading mode.

slides.title: The three question types
slides.body:
- **Words in Context** — which meaning does this specific word carry *here*? (Not its most common dictionary sense.)
- **Text Structure & Purpose** — what is this sentence/paragraph *doing* for the whole passage? (Its function, named as a verb.)
- **Cross-Text Connections** — how would the author of Text 2 respond to a specific point in Text 1? (Stance comparison.)

All three reward reading for **function**, not surface content — the skill you started building in Information & Ideas, now central.

slides.title: Words in Context is not a vocabulary quiz
slides.body:
> **Key idea:** the test measures the word's meaning *in this sentence's logic*, not the definition you'd give cold.

The most common trap is a familiar word used in a *secondary* sense. "The committee's **qualified** support" — "qualified" here means *limited/conditional*, not *certified* or *skilled*. If you read the choices first, the familiar meaning primes you and you fall in. The fix is a procedure (next), not more flashcards.

slides.title: Part 2 — Strategy a top scorer uses
Predict before you peek — the core procedure
slides.body: For every Words-in-Context item: (1) cover the answer choices; (2) read the sentence and the one before/after, tracking logic cues — contrast (*however, but, despite*), cause (*because, thus*), continuation (*and, moreover*); (3) say your *own* word that fits that logic; (4) *now* reveal choices and pick the closest synonym to **your** prediction. This inoculates you against the familiar-but-wrong-sense trap because your prediction came from the sentence, not from your prior associations. It is the single most reliable verbal technique on the test.

slides.title: Purpose questions: answer with a verb
slides.body: For "the main purpose of the underlined sentence is to ___", the credited answer is a **function verb**: *to qualify, to counter, to illustrate, to concede, to transition, to define*. If you can name what the sentence *does for its paragraph*, the right choice is obvious and the "accurately restates the sentence but isn't its purpose" trap collapses. Force yourself to produce the verb before reading choices.

slides.title: Cross-text: pin each stance in three words first
slides.body: Before comparing two short paired texts, write a ≤3-word stance for each author (e.g., *"pro, with caveats"* / *"skeptical"* / *"neutral-explanatory"*). Almost every Cross-Text question reduces to: would Author 2 **agree with**, **qualify**, or **reject** Author 1's *specific* point? Decide the stance relationship first; the answer follows mechanically. Skipping this step is why students find these 'hard'.

slides.title: Part 3 — Worked examples, end to end
Worked example 1 — Words-in-Context
slides.body:
Sentence: *"The committee's **qualified** support meant the proposal advanced, but only after major revisions."* Stem: as used, *qualified* most nearly means — (A) certified (B) limited/conditional (C) skilled (D) eligible.

Predict from logic first: *"but only after major revisions"* signals support that is **not full** → predicted word ≈ "partial/conditional."

slides.title: Worked example 1 — walking it
slides.body: Match prediction to choices: (B) limited/conditional aligns. (A) *certified* and (C) *skilled* are the everyday meanings of "qualified" — textbook familiar-sense traps, placed precisely to catch readers who skipped the prediction step. (D) *eligible* ignores the sentence's contrast. The technique didn't just find the answer; it *predicted which wrong answers the test would offer*. That is what mastery looks like.

question.question: Best first move on a Words-in-Context question?
options: Predict a word from the sentence's logic before reading choices
Pick the most common meaning of the word
question.explanation: Predicting from context first inoculates you against the SAT's favorite trap: the word's familiar-but-here-wrong sense.

slides.title: Worked example 2 — Purpose
slides.body: *Underlined sentence:* "Of course, a single study cannot settle the matter." *Stem:* its main purpose is to — choices include "summarize the study's findings" vs "acknowledge a limitation of the argument." The sentence *says* little; its **function** is concession/qualification. The summary choice is a *paraphrase trap* — accurate about content, wrong about role. Name the verb (*to concede/qualify*) and the credited choice is unambiguous.

slides.title: The Craft & Structure trap families
slides.body:
1. **Familiar-sense** (Words in Context) — the word's common meaning, wrong here.
2. **Paraphrase-not-purpose** — restates the sentence accurately but doesn't name its function.
3. **Stance-mismatch** (Cross-Text) — flips *qualify* vs *reject*, or *agree* vs *agree-with-reservations*.
4. **Scope creep** — a function that's too strong/broad for what the sentence actually does.

Eliminate by naming the trap, not by vibes.

question.question: Diagnose the mistake.
question.scenario: On a 'purpose of this sentence' question, a student picks a choice that accurately *restates what the sentence says*. They get it wrong.

rubricCriteria.description: distinguishes what a sentence SAYS from what it DOES (its function)
notes purpose questions need a functional verb (to counter/illustrate/qualify…)
recommends naming the sentence's job in the paragraph, not paraphrasing it

question.explanation: Purpose ≠ paraphrase. A choice can correctly summarize the sentence yet not name its *role*; that's the credited trap on structure/purpose items.

hints: Did Author 2 deny X works, or limit when it works?
slides.workedSolution: Cross-text answers hinge on stance precision: short-term-only evidence *qualifies* (accepts with a limit) rather than *rejects* (denies outright) or *agrees* (no reservation). Naming the stance verb picks the answer.

question.question: Two paired texts: Author 1 argues policy X works; Author 2 presents data that X works only short-term. Author 2 would most likely:
options: Qualify Author 1's claim, accepting it with an added limitation
question.explanation: "Works only short-term" concedes the effect but bounds it — a qualification, not a rejection or full agreement.

question.question: "Purpose" questions are best answered with:
options: A verb naming what the text does (qualify, counter, illustrate)
A summary of the text's content
question.explanation: Function is a verb. If you can say the sentence's job, the right option is the one matching that verb.

question.prompt: Teach back: why does 'predict, then match' beat 'read the choices first' on Words-in-Context — and what trap does it defeat?

rubricCriteria.description: prediction is built from the sentence's own logic/cues
matching to a prediction resists the familiar-but-wrong-sense trap
reading choices first primes you toward the common meaning

question.question: In your own words, state the difference between what a sentence *says* and what it *does*, with one example.

rubricCriteria.description: 'does' = its function in the paragraph (a verb role)
gives a concrete example distinguishing the two

slides.title: How it scores & what's next
slides.body: Craft & Structure is ~28% of Reading & Writing; the 'read for function' habit and the predict-then-match procedure are its whole game. Next, **Expression of Ideas** — you stop interpreting text and start *editing* it to hit a stated rhetorical goal, the fastest-improving points on the test.
